title: Building a RAG Engine From Scratch: No APIs, No Cloud
description: What actually clicked once I built the embedding-to-retrieval pipeline myself, locally, on an RTX 4060.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Building a RAG Engine From Scratch: No APIs, No Cloud

Spent today building a RAG engine from scratch. No APIs, no cloud, just an RTX 4060 and a lot of confusion. Understanding actually clicked once I stopped treating retrieval as a black box.

## The core realization

An AI doesn't 'search' the way Google does. It converts a question into a list of numbers, an embedding, and finds chunks of text whose numbers are geometrically close.

> Meaning is literally stored as geometry. Similar text becomes nearby vectors in space.

## The pipeline

1. Take real documents.
2. Chunk them smartly, since embedding an entire document as one vector loses meaning.
3. Convert each chunk into embeddings using a local model, `nomic-embed-text` via Ollama, at zero API cost.
4. Embed the incoming query the same way.
5. Compare using cosine similarity, essentially the angle between vectors.
6. Return the most relevant chunks.

## Running it locally

```bash
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
```

No paid APIs, no hosted vector DB, just local inference and local storage.

## What felt like magic

Typing a question and getting back the exact right chunk from a document the model had never seen before, in the traditional sense. That's semantic search. That's what RAG is built on.

## What's next

ChromaDB, FAISS, hybrid search, and rerankers are still ahead, but today's foundation makes all of that make sense now.

## Takeaway

If you're learning RAG, don't skip the fundamentals. Embeddings and chunking are the whole game.

title: What Overfitting Actually Taught Me About My First ML Model
description: 99% training accuracy, 58% validation accuracy, and a night of tweaking parameters before understanding why.
author: Akshay More
content:
# What Overfitting Actually Taught Me About My First ML Model

I was building my first ML model. Training accuracy: 99%. Validation accuracy: 58%. Classic overfitting.

## What overfitting actually is

Overfitting is when a model memorizes the training data so well that it fails on anything new. It's the equivalent of a student who mugs up last year's question paper word for word, then freezes when the exam has one new question. Perfect on what it already knows, a disaster in the real world.

## What I tried first (and why it didn't work)

- Changed the learning rate.
- Adjusted batch size.
- Tried different optimizers.

None of it worked, because none of it addressed why the model was memorizing instead of learning.

## The actual fixes

1. **Dropout** — randomly switches off neurons during training so the model can't just memorize, forcing it to learn actual patterns.
2. **Regularization (L1/L2)** — adds a penalty for complexity, discouraging the model from overfitting to noise.
3. **More data** — obvious, but the most effective lever. A model that has seen more examples generalizes better.
4. **Early stopping** — stop training once validation loss stops improving, instead of letting it over-study the training set.

## Takeaway

A model that only performs well on training data is useless. Generalization is everything, in ML and, honestly, in life.

title: The AI Opportunity Is Shifting: From Building to Organizing
description: A reality check on where AI leverage is actually moving as tools get cheaper and execution gets commoditized.
author: Akshay More
content:
# The AI Opportunity Is Shifting: From Building to Organizing

A reality check worth sitting with: the earliest phase of the AI opportunity has already peaked, and most people learning AI right now are optimizing for the wrong layer.

## What worked in 2023-2024

The early window rewarded execution. Offering AI services, building automations, selling implementation work, these were genuinely scarce skills, and early adopters captured real value because almost nobody else could do the work yet.

## Why that window is closing

The tools themselves are catching up:

- Cheaper access to capable models.
- Simpler interfaces that need less technical depth.
- Drag-and-drop automation replacing custom-built pipelines.

This is a familiar pattern in any maturing market: when execution gets easier, it gets replaceable, and replaceable skills compress margins. The moat that early builders had was never the AI itself, it was that building with it was still hard.

## Where the leverage is moving

The uncomfortable part is that doing AI is no longer the scarce skill. Millions of people are trying to pick up AI video, avatars, automation, and prompt engineering, and most of them are drowning in tutorials, not short on tools.

What they're actually short on is structure, a clear path through the noise, not another builder showing off a new workflow.

## The reality check

The next wave of winners in this space likely won't be the sharpest technicians. They'll be the people who can take a genuinely complex, fragmented landscape and make it legible for everyone else, the clearest educators and synthesizers, not just the fastest shippers.

## Takeaway

Execution skill still matters, but it's no longer the differentiator it was two years ago. If the tools are the commodity now, the value shifts to whoever can organize, teach, and make sense of them for people who are still catching up.

title: Building AI Agents with LangGraph
description: How I structured agent state, tools, and routing to keep an assistant reliable enough for real workflows.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Building AI Agents with LangGraph

A production agent should be predictable before it is impressive. I used LangGraph to make state, tools, and routing explicit so the system stays debuggable.

## Why I reached for LangGraph

- State is visible.
- Tool calls are intentional.
- Branches are easy to reason about.

> If you cannot explain the control flow in one minute, it is too magical for production.

## A small example

```ts
import { StateGraph } from '@langchain/langgraph'

const graph = new StateGraph()
  .addNode('planner', plannerNode)
  .addNode('tool', toolNode)
  .addEdge('planner', 'tool')
```

## What actually mattered

I leaned on tight prompts, short context windows, and clear fallbacks. The model can be creative; the product should remain boringly reliable.

![LangGraph sketch](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1515879218367-8466d910aaa4?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80)

## Final takeaway

Build the graph for the failure case first, then add intelligence on top.

title: Scaling AI Automation for Businesses
description: A practical look at batching, retries, and human-in-the-loop checks for automation that people can trust.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Scaling AI Automation for Businesses

Automation is useful only when it can fail gracefully. Once a workflow touches customers, reliability matters more than novelty.

## What helped

1. Queue work instead of firing everything at once.
2. Add explicit retries for transient errors.
3. Surface a manual review step for edge cases.

## A simple pattern

```ts
const result = await runWorkflow(input)
if (!result.ok) {
  await notifyHuman(result.reason)
}
```

## The real win

The strongest systems were the ones people could understand at a glance. Clarity beats cleverness when you are operating in production.

title: Deploying IntervuAI: Vercel, Railway, and the Small Config Fights
description: What broke when shipping a LangGraph interview simulator to production, and the two config fixes that mattered.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Deploying IntervuAI: Vercel, Railway, and the Small Config Fights

IntervuAI is an adaptive interview simulator built on LangGraph, FastAPI, and Groq. The code worked locally. Deployment is where the real debugging started.

## Vercel misread the project

Vercel auto-detected the repo as a FastAPI serverless function because the backend lived at the root alongside the frontend. The fix was simple once found: set the Root Directory to `frontend` in the project settings so Vercel only builds the React app.

## Railway wanted lowercase

The backend config file needs to be named `railway.toml`, not `Railway.toml`. Case-sensitive filesystems on the build server silently ignored the capitalized version, and Railway fell back to defaults that didn't match the app.

## What shipped

- Frontend on Vercel, root directory scoped correctly.
- Backend on Railway, config picked up after the rename.
- LangGraph + Groq handling adaptive question difficulty during the interview.

## Takeaway

Most of deployment debugging isn't your code. It's platform assumptions about your repo's shape.

title: Fine-Tuning Qwen2.5-7B on an 8GB GPU
description: Why a GGUF model can't be fine-tuned directly, and how QLoRA through Unsloth made a single 8GB card enough.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Fine-Tuning Qwen2.5-7B on an 8GB GPU

I needed to fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B on a small astrology dataset and deploy it with vLLM. The first mistake was assuming I could fine-tune the GGUF model I already had pulled through Ollama.

## Why GGUF didn't work

GGUF is a quantized, inference-only format. There is no gradient path back through it. Training needs the original Hugging Face safetensors weights, not the compressed artifact Ollama serves.

## The actual pipeline

- Pull the base model in HF safetensors format.
- Apply QLoRA using Unsloth, which keeps the base weights in 4-bit and only trains small adapter layers.
- Merge or keep adapters separate depending on the deployment target.

> An 8GB card cannot hold a 7B model's full gradients. It can absolutely hold its LoRA adapters.

## Deployment

```bash
pip install vllm
vllm serve ./merged-model --max-model-len 4096
```

## Takeaway

Quantized inference formats and trainable formats are not the same thing, even when they come from the same base model. Check which one you actually have before writing the training loop.

title: Building a Job Application Tracker with n8n, Ollama, and Notion
description: Self-hosting an automation that reads Gmail, classifies applications with a local LLM, and logs them to Notion.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Building a Job Application Tracker with n8n, Ollama, and Notion

I was applying to enough roles that manually tracking status in a spreadsheet stopped working. So I built a self-hosted n8n workflow: Gmail in, a local LLM to classify, Notion out.

## The stack

- n8n running in Docker, self-hosted on port 5680.
- Gmail OAuth2 to pull application-related emails.
- Ollama running qwen2.5:7b locally for classification.
- Notion as the tracker database.

## Where it broke

The Basic LLM Chain node in n8n wraps calls through LangChain internally, and that wrapper silently overrode the custom JSON prompt I was sending. The model kept returning conversational text instead of structured output.

> If a node abstracts away the request, it can also abstract away the part of the request you actually needed.

## The fix

I dropped the Basic LLM Chain node entirely and used a plain HTTP Request node pointed directly at Ollama's API. That gave me full control over the prompt and the response format.

```json
{
  "model": "qwen2.5:7b",
  "prompt": "Classify this email as: applied, interview, rejected, offer. Return JSON only.",
  "stream": false
}
```

## Status

Gmail ingestion and classification are working end-to-end. Notion write-back is the piece I'm finishing next.

title: How I Built My AI Portfolio
description: The design decisions, content structure, and motion system behind a portfolio that feels calm instead of loud.
author: Akshay More
content:
# How I Built My AI Portfolio

This portfolio was designed to feel quiet, premium, and intentional. The goal was not to impress with noise. The goal was to make the work easy to scan.

## Design rules

- Keep typography in charge.
- Let whitespace do the heavy lifting.
- Use motion only where it clarifies state.

## Structure

The homepage leads with a simple story, then moves into recent work, writing, and contact. That order keeps the page readable on mobile and desktop.

> Clean design is usually the result of fewer decisions, not more decoration.

## Result

The final build feels closer to a developer journal than a flashy landing page, which is exactly what I wanted.

title: Writing a Binance Futures Trading Bot Without a Wrapper Library
description: Building a CLI trading bot on raw REST calls and HMAC-SHA256 signing, and the demo API key issue that ate an afternoon.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Writing a Binance Futures Trading Bot Without a Wrapper Library

For a Binance Futures Testnet assignment, the requirement was direct REST calls with manual HMAC-SHA256 signing, no `python-binance` or similar wrapper. That constraint turned out to be the interesting part.

## What the bot supports

- MARKET, LIMIT, and STOP order types.
- A mock demo mode for testing logic without hitting the API.
- Unit tests covering signature generation and order payload construction.

## The signature

```python
import hmac, hashlib

def sign(query_string: str, secret: str) -> str:
    return hmac.new(secret.encode(), query_string.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
```

## The error that ate an afternoon

Every request returned a `-2015` invalid API key error, even with keys copied correctly from the Binance Futures Testnet dashboard. The actual cause: the demo trading environment needs keys generated specifically from `demo.binance.com`, not the regular testnet key generator. Two systems that look identical, issuing incompatible keys.

## Takeaway

When an error message says invalid credentials but the credentials look right, check whether you're even pointed at the right environment before touching the code.

title: Taking SnapClass from Streamlit Prototype to a Dockerized API
description: Splitting a Streamlit prototype into a FastAPI service, containerizing both, and wiring up CI/CD.
author: Akshay More
content:
# Taking SnapClass from Streamlit Prototype to a Dockerized API

SnapClass started as a Streamlit prototype, which is great for demoing an idea and bad for anything that needs a stable API surface. Productionizing it meant splitting the logic out from the UI.

## The split

- A FastAPI service exposing the core functionality as a REST API, running on port 8000.
- Streamlit kept as a thin UI layer on port 8501, calling the API instead of holding logic itself.
- Both containerized separately with Docker so they scale and deploy independently.

## What broke along the way

- A `ModuleNotFoundError` traced back to inconsistent package paths between the Streamlit and FastAPI containers.
- `webrtcvad` failing to build inside Docker, needing the right system-level build dependencies added to the image.
- Streamlit version incompatibilities between what worked locally and what the container pulled.
- Supabase UUID and integer type mismatches that only showed up once real data hit the tables.

## CI/CD

GitHub Actions runs the build and test steps on push, so a broken container never reaches deployment silently.

## Takeaway

A prototype and a product have different jobs. Separating them early made each piece easier to reason about, even though it meant more moving parts up front.
